profile.level: L2 (cumulative L1 + L2) as a floor, plus named L3 requirements

profile.shape: A level is a floor rather than a target. The controls §10.9 names are scattered across L1, L2 and L3, so the profile is L2 plus named pull-ups plus an addendum for what the standard does not carry at any level.
profile.applicability_rule: A chapter is in scope unless it is excluded, and an exclusion carries a reason. A conditional exclusion carries a trigger, the way §15s deferred rows do. **The assurance value of a baseline is in the exclusions being recorded, not in the inclusions passing** — an unrecorded exclusion is how a profile becomes decoration.
profile.what_the_standard_does_not_cover: ASVS 5.0.0 has one requirement mentioning browser storage, and none mentioning Trusted Types, service workers or offline operation. That is a fact about what the standard is for rather than a criticism of it, and it is why the addendum exists.

V1.name: Encoding and Sanitization
V1.why: The client renders user-authored markdown into the DOM. §10.9 makes this the chapter that matters most: same-origin code is inside the end-to-end boundary, so an injection here is key exfiltration rather than defacement.

V2.name: Validation and Business Logic
V2.why: Thin — the CRDT merges and there is little business logic to subvert — but import parses a file the user supplies (§9.2), and that is the untrusted input this product actually has.

V3.name: Web Frontend Security
V3.why: Where §10.9's named controls live. Four of this chapter's L3 requirements are pulled up, because a product whose origin holds the keys should not take frontend hardening at the level a brochure site takes it.

V4.name: API and Web Service
V4.why: The account service and the relay. Nothing to verify until they exist; the relay is content-blind (§7.2), so most of this chapter lands on a component that cannot read what it carries.

V5.name: File Handling
V5.why: Import and export are file handling (§9.1, §9.2). There is no upload and no server-side file storage, so the chapter applies at its client-side edge only.

V6.name: Authentication
V6.why: The largest applicability question in the profile, and it is not answered by 'the feature is absent'. §15 row 12 selected a passkey-only account credential and rows 13 and 14 rejected stretching, so this chapter's password, lockout and credential-recovery requirements are inapplicable because the design chose a shape they do not contemplate. Each has to be recorded with that reason at verification, or the chapter reads as cherry-picked.

V7.name: Session Management
V7.why: Partially, and the boundary is already drawn: §13.9 says a local slot is not a session and reopening one grants no relay token and no account session. Session requirements bind the account session; they do not bind the slot.

V8.name: Authorization
V8.why: The authorization lineage (§13.5). Service-authoritative by construction, which is what most of this chapter asks for.

V9.name: Self-contained Tokens
V9.why: Self-contained tokens apply only if the relay admission token turns out to be one. §13.2 fixes what the token may do and not its shape.
V9.trigger: The relay admission token being selected as a self-contained token rather than an opaque handle.

V10.name: OAuth and OIDC
V10.why: There is no OAuth and no OIDC anywhere in the design. The account service authenticates its own credential (§13.9) and issues its own admission tokens (§13.2); no third-party identity provider is contemplated, and adding one would be a product decision with its own document. **This is 36 of 345 requirements — over a tenth of the standard — excluded on one sentence**, which is exactly why the sentence is here.

V11.name: Cryptography
V11.why: Applicable, and the one chapter where the floor sits below what is already selected: §13.10's suite and §15's fifteen constructions are more specific than this chapter asks for, each with generated vectors, and reviews 3a and 3b are a stronger control than a checklist. That is worth stating plainly rather than as a boast — it means V11 is where a *conflict* would surface if the profile and the design disagreed.

V12.name: Secure Communication
V12.why: TLS to the relay and the account service, and §10.9's origin checks on the transport upgrade. The development relay does not satisfy this chapter and is not meant to (§7.2).

V13.name: Configuration
V13.why: Build and deployment configuration: dependency integrity, what reaches the built artifact, and what the deployment exposes. Most of it is checkable from the build rather than by inspection.

V14.name: Data Protection
V14.why: Data protection, and it holds the profile's one deviation: V14.3.3 forbids sensitive data in browser storage, and this product's entire content lives in IndexedDB. See `deviations`.

V15.name: Secure Coding and Architecture
V15.why: Dependencies and coding practice. Four of its L3 requirements are pulled up, because a dependency in the key-holding origin is a party inside the end-to-end boundary (§10.9) rather than a supply-chain abstraction.

V16.name: Security Logging and Error Handling
V16.why: Service-side logging, and it is a real cost of choosing L2: the chapter has no L1 requirements and sixteen at L2, so the level choice pulls the whole of it in. PRD §7.11's allowlist and §16.4's inventory rows are what it will be verified against.

V17.name: WebRTC
V17.why: There is no WebRTC. Peer-to-peer is deferred, and PRD §2.3 gates it on four measured conditions rather than on intent.
V17.trigger: PRD §2.3's four conditions all being met and peer-to-peer being built.

pull_ups.why: DOM clobbering. L3 for an ordinary application; here the thing clobbered code reaches is a key handle.
A CSP violation-reporting location. Without it the policy is enforced and unobserved, and the first thing it blocks is also the first thing nobody hears about.
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy. A key-holding origin should not share a browsing-context group with anything.

§10.9's first named control, at L3 in the standard: external assets only with Subresource Integrity. The profile goes further — the addendum forbids remote subresources outright — so this is pulled up to be superseded rather than skipped.
Documenting risky components. L3 because most applications can treat a dependency as a supply-chain abstraction; one inside the end-to-end boundary is a party to it.
The same for dangerous functionality, and §10.10 already names the one instance.
Transitive dependencies from the expected repository, and no dependency-confusion exposure. This is §10.9's 'dependency integrity' in the standard's own words.
Additional protections around what the two documentation requirements above identify. Pulled up with them, because documenting a risk and doing nothing about it is the failure mode of documenting it.

deviations.what: Forbids sensitive data in browser storage, excepting session tokens.
deviations.position: Not met as written, and cannot be: the entire content of the application is user data in IndexedDB. That is what a local-first application is.
deviations.compensating_control: Every record is sealed under a content-key generation before it is written, with the key material held as a non-extractable handle and never present in a store (§6.1, §13.2, §13.3). §11.1s no-plaintext-at-rest test inspects a profile snapshot at genesis, at Local, at Account and after deletion, retention expiry and migration, so the claim is exercised rather than asserted.
deviations.note: ASVS 5.0.0 has **one** requirement mentioning browser storage and **none** mentioning Trusted Types, service workers or offline operation. The standard does not model an application of this shape, and the honest response is a recorded deviation plus the addendum below — not a level chosen high enough to look thorough.

addendum.control: No remote subresource in the key-holding origin. Not "with SRI" — none.
addendum.why: Same-origin code is inside the end-to-end boundary, so a third-party asset is a party added to it. SRI pins a byte string and does not remove the party.

addendum.control: Trusted Types enforced where the platform supports it.
addendum.why: ASVS 5.0.0 has no requirement mentioning Trusted Types. §10.9 names it, and it is the one control that turns DOM-sink injection from a review obligation into an enforcement.
addendum.planned_check: The web application is verified as part of the cryptographic boundary

addendum.control: Service-worker update integrity: the worker that can serve every future load is replaced only from the origin, over a checked artifact.
addendum.why: ASVS 5.0.0 has no requirement mentioning service workers. A PWA that caches its own shell has a persistent code path the standard does not model.

addendum.control: Everything an app-managed store holds is ciphertext, from genesis, on every device.
addendum.why: The compensating control for V14.3.3, stated as a requirement in its own right so the profile does not depend on a deviation entry to carry it.

addendum.control: No control may be weakened by being offline, and no control may require the network to hold.
addendum.why: The product is offline-first (§7.1), so a control that only holds while connected is not a control. ASVS assumes a server is reachable; here it frequently is not, and §13.9 already turns on that distinction.

verification: Selected in Stage 0; verified before Stage 4 ships (§13.11 level 2, sequencing §3.7). A1 is verified now, by scripts/check-origin-isolation.mjs inside `pnpm build`. The rest name their method here and acquire their check with the stage that makes them real.
